Waiver moves, by title odds

Each pickup is priced in P(win the title) on the same simulated seasons: claiming now, against waiting and claiming only if he breaks out (you win that claim when your priority beats the other managers who also want him), less what your waiver priority is worth on future claims. Passing is not free: if he breaks out, a rival claims him, and what that does to your title odds is counted. Each move is priced on its own; make one, then refresh. Assumes about a third of active managers chase any one breakout. Injured free agents are priced as IR stashes: no roster spot until he is back, with the chance he never is.

Waiver plans: several moves together

Moves interact -- two backs chasing one lineup spot are worth less together, two dead roster spots turned into a starter and his handcuff can be worth more -- so every combination of two or three pickups and drops is screened, and the best priced in title odds against standing pat and against the best single move. Make the plan when it beats that single move by more than the simulation noise; a close call when by less.

No plan beats the best single move; make that one and refresh.

Every free agent who could start for you this week, added to your roster with your best lineup rebuilt around him and scored against your opponent on the same simulated games as your lineup as it stands -- the chance you win this week with him, against without. The title columns are the whole move in points of P(title), on the season simulation: Wk is this week's win -- the P(win) gain times what this game swings your title odds; Rest is every week after, his value less that of the player you drop; Net is the two together, less the waiver priority a claim spends. The verdict goes on Net: a pickup that wins this week can still cost more later than it gains now. If he is on waivers, the claim has to clear before his game.

Most valuable players

Value is points above a waiver pickup at his position, summed over weeks 9-17: what he is simulated to score each week he plays, less what the pickup would. Weeks he misses (byes, injuries, a reported timeline) count nothing, so a hurt star drops down. Upside is that value in his best tenth of simulated seasons: a breakout, a bigger role, a clean bill of health. Pickup level a game: QB 14.5, RB 7.4, WR 9.4, TE 8.6, K 9.2, D/ST 11.1. RoS/g is his season value a game and Δwk its move since last week (green up, red down, yellow flat; deeper is bigger -- tap Δwk for the risers, again for the fallers), Wk this week's projection, G games expected, Range his points a week (10th-90th percentile) and Mkt what the rest of the league sees him worth a game (those three on wider screens). Tap a column to sort; your players are highlighted. Tap a player's name for his game log: points, snap share and stat line, week by week.

Best D/ST and K for this matchup

Free agents and your own, each swapped into your recommended lineup and scored against your opponent on the same correlated simulations. Each player's future is simulated (role drift, injuries, byes, the next man up taking over -- graded on 2022-2025 seasons it was not fitted to: points per game land in its middle half half the time, early form carries on as far as it really did, and what a manager can see of a player moves as much, and means as little, as a real projection did); every team starts its best lineup each week on what it could see then; the season is played on the real schedule and the playoffs on the real bracket. Rosters are held as they stand. The small ranges are 95% intervals for the simulation's own noise (Wilson): what a rerun could move the number by -- not whether the model's view of the season is right. Power is record-blind: the share of the other teams' scores a team beats in an average remaining week (all-play), from the same simulation and the same fading of team strength, so a team with a bad record and a strong roster ranks high here while its title odds stay low. Pts/wk ahead is the expected points a week for the rest of the regular season (a little closer together than raw projections: managers' waiver moves level rosters), so far what the team has scored a week in the weeks counted; a big gap between the two means the roster has changed or the points came on luck. Tap a column heading to sort.

Where this week's projections come from

Each player's number blends, where he has one from each:

Each weight is the one that would have been most accurate on this season's finished games, pulled toward its starting value until enough are graded. Tap a player's name for his game log. RoS/g: points a game when he plays, with its move since last week (green up, red down, yellow flat; deeper is bigger: under 0.3, 0.3–1, 1–2, over 2). Pts/wk: simulated points a remaining week, after injuries, byes, lost jobs and the next man up, with its 10th–90th percentile beneath. Title: points of your title odds lost without him, his spot filled from the wire, on the same seasons the hub prices every move on (grey: inside the noise). Mkt: what other managers see him worth a game; green above ours (sell), red below (hold).

Waiver moves, by title odds

Each pickup is priced in P(win the title) on the same simulated seasons: claiming now, against waiting and claiming only if he breaks out (you win that claim when your priority beats the other managers who also want him), less what your waiver priority is worth on future claims. Passing is not free: if he breaks out, a rival claims him, and what that does to your title odds is counted. Each move is priced on its own; make one, then refresh. Assumes about a third of active managers chase any one breakout. Injured free agents are priced as IR stashes: no roster spot until he is back, with the chance he never is.

No free agent raises your title odds enough to be worth a move.

Waiver plans: several moves together

Moves interact -- two backs chasing one lineup spot are worth less together, two dead roster spots turned into a starter and his handcuff can be worth more -- so every combination of two or three pickups and drops is screened, and the best priced in title odds against standing pat and against the best single move. Make the plan when it beats that single move by more than the simulation noise; a close call when by less.

No plan beats the best single move; make that one and refresh.

Pickups for this matchup

Every free agent who could start for you this week, added to your roster with your best lineup rebuilt around him and scored against your opponent on the same simulated games as your lineup as it stands -- the chance you win this week with him, against without. The title columns are the whole move in points of P(title), on the season simulation: Wk is this week's win -- the P(win) gain times what this game swings your title odds; Rest is every week after, his value less that of the player you drop; Net is the two together, less the waiver priority a claim spends. The verdict goes on Net: a pickup that wins this week can still cost more later than it gains now. If he is on waivers, the claim has to clear before his game.

Most valuable players

Value is points above a waiver pickup at his position, summed over weeks 9-17: what he is simulated to score each week he plays, less what the pickup would. Weeks he misses (byes, injuries, a reported timeline) count nothing, so a hurt star drops down. Upside is that value in his best tenth of simulated seasons: a breakout, a bigger role, a clean bill of health. Pickup level a game: QB 17.8, RB 5.7, WR 7.3, TE 6.9, K 9.5, D/ST 9.0. RoS/g is his season value a game and Δwk its move since last week (green up, red down, yellow flat; deeper is bigger -- tap Δwk for the risers, again for the fallers), Wk this week's projection, G games expected, Range his points a week (10th-90th percentile) and Mkt what the rest of the league sees him worth a game (those three on wider screens). Each player's future is simulated (role drift, injuries, byes, the next man up taking over -- graded on 2022-2025 seasons it was not fitted to: points per game land in its middle half half the time, early form carries on as far as it really did, and what a manager can see of a player moves as much, and means as little, as a real projection did); every team starts its best lineup each week on what it could see then; the season is played on the real schedule and the playoffs on the real bracket. Rosters are held as they stand. The small ranges are 95% intervals for the simulation's own noise (Wilson): what a rerun could move the number by -- not whether the model's view of the season is right. Power is record-blind: the share of the other teams' scores a team beats in an average remaining week (all-play), from the same simulation and the same fading of team strength, so a team with a bad record and a strong roster ranks high here while its title odds stay low. Pts/wk ahead is the expected points a week for the rest of the regular season (a little closer together than raw projections: managers' waiver moves level rosters), so far what the team has scored a week in the weeks counted; a big gap between the two means the roster has changed or the points came on luck. Tap a column heading to sort.

Playoff odds by final record -- 5 wins: 0%, 6 wins: 0%, 7 wins: 13%, 8 wins: 88%, 9 wins: 100%, 10 wins: 100%, 11 wins: 100%. Each game is flipped in every simulated season with everything else held as it fell, so the swing is what that one result is worth, including what it does to the opponent's record. Your lineup is always set to win the week in front of you; this is about where the season turns.
